sheets.summary:
What is the significance of Rosh Chodesh being the first mitzvah listed in the Torah? 
We know that within time itself are certain 'energies', that even the Avot were able to celebrate the holidays because of a certain potential that every time has to express that specific holiday. However, the Jewish people actually have been given the ability to "create" and sanctify the new month. This has a powerful lesson in it - that HaShem gives the Jewish people a large role in the world. 
The Jewish people are to HaShem like the sun is to the moon, so to speak. The sun is always in its perfection and completion. However, its light is only reflected into the world during the night according to the amount that the moon is reflecting. So, while still for a short while we remain in this galut, it is up the Jewish people to reveal the G-dly light inherent in all of existence. That is why it is understood amongst the holy seforim that the Jewish people are the embodiment of the Shechina, which allows the infinite light of HaShem to be expressed in this world. 
As an ending point, we know that Rosh Chodesh is specifically a women's holiday, as the women remained faithful to HaShem during the golden calf incident. When our emunah is strong, that even when the moon is just a sliver we know that it will soon be full, we are able to reveal the G-dly light within the world.

en.title: God’s Dual Nature in Creation
en.prompt: The world contains both judgment and mercy — but, according to some interpreters, that was not always God’s plan for creation. Rashi, in his renowned 11th-century commentary on the Torah, interprets the use of different names of God in Genesis as reflecting different aspects of God in the creation of the world.

description.en: The opening two [chapters](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=he) of the Torah describe how God created the world in six days and rested on the seventh. These chapters are some of the most analyzed words in the Jewish textual tradition and serve as a basis for discussions of topics like [human dignity](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/human-dignity?tab=admin), God's role in the world, Shabbat, and humankind's responsibility for continuing the creation process and caring for the world.

*Sheratzim* are small creatures that creep or crawl, described and listed in Leviticus [11:29-30](https://www.sefaria.org/Leviticus.11.31?ven=Tanakh:_The_Holy_Scriptures,_published_by_JPS&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Their corpses convey impurity to people and vessels when encountered in specific ways.

Eating features from the outset of the Torah in the story of the garden of Eden, where Adam and Eve's [consumption](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.3.6?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) of forbidden fruit shapes human history. Food serves as a central theme in many other biblical stories: Patriarchs and matriarchs [leave](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.12.10?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&sbsq=%D7%95%D7%99%D7%94%D7%99%20%D7%A8%D7%A2%D7%91%20%D7%91%D7%90%D7%A8%D7%A5&with=SidebarSearch&lang2=en) their homes during [famines](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.26.1?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&sbsq=%D7%95%D7%99%D7%94%D7%99%20%D7%A8%D7%A2%D7%91%20%D7%91%D7%90%D7%A8%D7%A5&with=SidebarSearch&lang2=en) in search of food to eat, Esau sells his birthright to eat a [bowl of soup](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.25.30?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&sbsq=%D7%94%D7%9C%D7%A2%D7%99%D7%98%D7%A0%D7%99&with=SidebarSearch&lang2=en), and the people of Israel repeatedly [complain](https://www.sefaria.org/Numbers.11.4?ven=hebrew|Tanach_with_Ta%27amei_Hamikra&lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) about food in the desert. Jewish texts explore many commandments and practices surrounding food, including feeding the hungry, reciting blessings before and after eating, observing the laws of kashrut, and eating certain foods during specific occasions (like matzah on Passover, for example).

description.he: על פי התלמוד, מאז ימי אדם הראשון ועד נֹח נהגה האנושות בצמחונות. במקורות יהודיים אחרים מלמדים כי ההיתר לאכול בשר שניתן לבסוף מידי אלוהים היה פשרה מוסרית בלבד, ועל כן ההלכה מגבילה את סוגי הבשר המותרים לאכילה ואת הדרכים המותרות לאכילתו.
description.en: According to the Talmud, from Adam to Noah humans practiced vegetarianism (tzimchonut). In the Jewish sources, God's eventual permission to eat meat is often seen as nothing more than an ethical compromise and Jewish law restricts the type and way that meat is eaten.

The Leviathan is a giant sea creature that features in several places throughout the Jewish textual tradition. In the Bible, it is mentioned a total of six times: in the books of Isaiah, Psalms, and Job. Rabbinic literature describes how God created the Leviathan [during the creation of the world](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.74b.5?lang=en&with=all&lang2=en) and how, in a future world to come, the [righteous will feast from the flesh of the Leviathan](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.75a.4?lang=en&with=all&lang2=en).

Light, both physical and metaphorical, features prominently throughout the Jewish textual tradition. Among other instances, light is the first thing God creates in the book of Genesis, is a focus of the holiday of [Chanukkah](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/chanukkah?tab=sources), and is a central concept in kabbalastic literature, representing divine emanations.

God is central in traditional Jewish texts. God [utters the world into existence](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.1?lang=bi&with=Translations&lang2=en) from the outset of Genesis, and Rambam, in the opening to his halakhic masterpiece, Mishnah Torah, explains that belief in God is the [foundation of all foundations](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishneh_Torah%2C_Foundations_of_the_Torah.1.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). description.en: Eve was the first woman, the "mother of all," created by being separated from [Adam's](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/adam?tab=sources) body. In the [garden of Eden](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/garden-of-eden?tab=sources), the snake convinced Eve to try the forbidden fruit of the [tree of knowledge](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/the-tree-of-knowledge?tab=sources), from which she also gave to Adam. The result was that they were both expelled from the garden and that she and all of womankind would be cursed to endure difficult [childbirths](https://www.sefaria.org/topics/birth?tab=sources) even as they desire their husbands, to whom they are subject.
description.he: חוה היא האישה הראשונה מבנות מינה ואם כל חי. היא נוצרה מצלעו של אדם והופרדה ממנו. הנחש בגן עדן שכנע אותה לטעום מפרי עץ הדעת, וממנו האכילה גם את אדם. בעקבות זאת גורשו שניהם מגן עדן, ובנות מינה קוללו בלידות קשות ובשיעבוד לגברים.

description.en: Angels – often understood as messengers of God or supernatural beings – appear widely throughout Tanakh, rabbinic literature, kabbalistic literature, and Jewish liturgy. In the Torah, they often convey messages, like when an angel [informs Hagar](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.16.7?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) that she will give birth to a son, or when an angel [tells Abraham](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.22.11?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en) not to sacrifice Isaac. In the books of the Prophets, angels are also featured as part of visions and prophecies. Later Jewish texts expand on the nature of angels, describing the roles and attributes of specific angels and how the belief in angels shapes certain Jewish [practices](https://www.sefaria.org/Shalom_Aleichem.1?lang=bi).

description.he: השם ישראל הוא שמו השני של יעקב אבינו, שם שניתן לו מפי מלאך, ועל שמו נקראו בני ישראל שכוללים את שבטי ישראל, צאצאיו של יעקב. על פי התנ"ך ארץ ישראל הובטחה לאבות ולבני ישראל לאחר יציאת מצרים ובה שכנו ממלכות ישראל ויהודה. מקורות חז"ליים והלכתיים שונים מבטאים את קשר הדוק בין הקיום היהודי וארץ ישראל על ידי הלכות ייחודיות לארץ ישראל ודרשות בחשיבותה הערכית ובשבחה של אדמת ארץ ישראל. מדינת ישראל, בה יושבים יהודים בארץ ישראל במדינתם לאחר אלפיים שנות גלות מבטאת עבור רבים התגשמות של חזון הנביאים. חשיבות הקמתה והשמירה עליה מופיעים במקורות יהדות החל מראשית הציונות במאה ה-19 ועד ימינו.

description.en: God is central in traditional Jewish texts. God [utters the world into existence](https://www.sefaria.org/Genesis.1.1?lang=bi&with=Translations&lang2=en) from the outset of Genesis, and Rambam, in the opening to his halakhic masterpiece, Mishnah Torah, explains that belief in God is the [foundation of all foundations](https://www.sefaria.org/Mishneh_Torah%2C_Foundations_of_the_Torah.1.1?lang=bi&with=all&lang2=en). Countless Jewish sources discuss God's essence, the constraints of using human language to describe a transcendent Being, and how people are to develop relationships with God.

description.en: Chanukkah is an eight-day winter holiday commemorating the Jewish victory over the Seleucid Greek oppressors in 164 BCE. It is widely known as the "Festival of Lights" due to the practice of lighting a candle or oil lamp each night of the holiday. This ritual recalls the miracle of the oil, in which a small container of oil for the Temple menorah lasted for eight nights, after it was expected to last for only one.
description.he: חג החנוכה הוא חג בן שמונה ימים החל בחודש כסלו בחודשי החורף, לזכר נצחון היהודים על היוונים במאה שנייה לפני הספירה. הוא מוכר כ"חג האור" משום שמדליקים בו נרות בכל ימות החג. הדלקת הנרות מזכירה את הנס שבו השמן במנורת המקדש הספיק לשמונה לילות - למרות שהיה אמור להספיק רק ללילה אחד.

en.title: The Quality of Mercy
en.prompt: God’s four-letter name is commonly associated with the divine aspect of mercy or compassion, in contrast with the name Elohim, which is is associated with the severe aspect of justice. Eleventh-century northern French rabbi and commentator Rashi, in light of this distinction, discusses why it might be that first chapter of Genesis exclusively uses Elohim, and only in the second chapter does the Tetragrammaton first appear.

description.he: ארבע אותיות אלה (שבאנגלית נכתבות YHVH) מייצגות את 'השם המפורש' של אלוהים. מסורת יהודית עתיקה אוסרת להגות בקול את השם, ולכן אופן ההגייה המקורי של מילה זו אינו ברור.  במקום זאת, ישנן מגוון של מילים שמחליפות את השם המפורש כמו "אדוניי" ו"השם" בהתאם להקשר.
description.en: The Hebrew letters ‘yud,’ ‘hey,’ ‘vav,’ and ‘hey’ (in English, YHVH) form what is known as the Tetragrammaton, or God’s four-letter name. Given the longstanding Jewish prohibition against speaking God’s name aloud, the word’s original pronunciation is unclear, and it is traditionally not pronounced as written. Instead, a variety of substitutes are used - like “Adonai” (“My Lord”) and “Hashem” (“The Name”) - depending on the context.
